html:
The Chagatai Khanate was the Mongol state in Central Asia ruled by Chagatai, the second son of Genghis Khan, and his descendants. It covered Transoxiana, the Seven Rivers country and the Tarim Basin, between the Amu Darya and the Altai.

It was one of the four great parts of the Mongol Empire and went its own way after 1259. Over time its Mongol rulers took up Turkic speech and Islam, though Mongolian stayed in use for official papers into the 1300s.

In the 1340s the khanate split in two:

  • In the west, in Transoxiana, Turkic emirs held real power behind puppet khans. One of them, Timur, rose to build his own empire from 1370.
  • In the east, called Moghulistan, the khan Tughlugh Timur converted to Islam around 1354. Chagatai khans ruled there and in the Tarim oases until the late 1600s, when the Dzungars took over.

The Chagatai language, the literary Turkic of Central Asia used by poets like Ali-Shir Nava'i and by Babur, the founder of the Mughal Empire, takes its name from the khanate.
